analysis.one_liner: Replaces the federal income tax with a 15 percent national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 18 cosponsors but never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died in committee when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, estate tax, gift tax, and several excise taxes, and replace them with a 15 percent tax on everything consumers buy. Businesses and exporters would pay no tax on their purchases, states would collect the tax for a fee, and the IRS would be shut down. Low-income families would get a rebate covering the tax they would owe up to the poverty level, but every dollar spent above that — including on a new home — would be taxed.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: the income tax (including taxes on capital gains and wages) and the estate and gift taxes disappear, and a consumption tax only applies to what someone actually spends, so money saved or invested goes untaxed. Families at or below the poverty line are protected by a full rebate. State governments gain a 1 percent fee for collecting the tax, and retailers get administrative credits for filing.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal income tax, the estate and gift taxes, and certain excise taxes, effective July 1, 2001.
Imposes a 15 percent tax on consumption instead, with no tax on property or services purchased for a business purpose or for export.
Provides a 'family consumption refund' that rebates the tax a family would owe up to the federal poverty level, delivered through each paycheck.
Has administering states collect the tax in exchange for a 1 percent administration fee, and bars any appropriations for the IRS after fiscal year 2003.

analysis.who_pays: Every consumer pays 15 cents on the dollar on purchases, on top of existing state sales taxes, and the burden falls hardest — as a share of income — on working families who spend nearly everything they earn. Homebuyers would owe 15 percent on a new home (payable over 30 years with interest), and banking, brokerage, and insurance fees would be taxed. Government purchases would also be taxed.

drawbacks.text: The family rebate fully offsets the tax only up to the federal poverty line; all consumption above that level is taxed at the full 15 percent, so a family spending twice the poverty level pays substantially more of its income in tax than under the income tax.

The bill repeals the estate and gift taxes and taxes only what is spent, so households living on accumulated wealth or investment income would pay far less than under the income tax they would no longer face.

Purchases of a new principal residence are taxed at 15 percent, payable in annual installments over 30 years with interest, and financial intermediation services — banking, brokerage, and insurance fees — are also taxed, raising the cost of homes and financial services.
A family member must have a bona fide Social Security number and be a lawful resident to count toward the rebate, excluding some households from full protection.
The bill ends IRS funding after fiscal 2003 and requires states to rewrite their own sales taxes to conform to the federal tax in order to collect it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending annual income tax filing and the estate tax is a real appeal, and the poverty-level rebate is a genuine effort to shield the poorest families. But the core trade is structural: it moves the federal tax burden from a system that taxes income — progressively, including investment income and large estates — to one that taxes spending at a flat 15 percent on top of state sales taxes. Families that spend most of what they earn would pay a larger share of their income in tax; households living on savings and inherited wealth would pay less. The 15 percent rate is measured against payments that include the tax itself, so the visible markup at the register would be closer to 17.6 percent. The rebate helps at the bottom but does nothing for the broad middle, and a 15 percent tax on a new home (spread over 30 years) would substantially raise housing costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, so it expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Billy Tauzin introduced the bill on April 15, 1999 with 18 original cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and, for portions within its jurisdiction, to the Rules Committee.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
The bill's 18 cosponsors included 15 Republicans and 3 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with high investment income and large estates are better off, because the income, capital gains, and estate taxes they would have lost under the bill all remained in force. The existing income tax system — and the tax preparation industry built around it — also continued unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: Support was largely Republican — 15 of the 18 cosponsors were Republicans, with 3 Democrats — and no floor vote ever occurred to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill repeals the income tax, capital gains taxation, and the estate and gift taxes, and taxes only consumption, so households that save or live on accumulated wealth pay dramatically less. The rebate shields families only up to the poverty line, so the tax burden shifts toward those who spend most of what they earn.

States that adopt a conforming sales tax would administer and collect the federal tax and keep a 1 percent administration fee. They gain revenue and a fee, but must rewrite their own sales tax laws to conform.

Retailers must register, collect, and remit the tax monthly, but receive an administrative credit (the greater of $200 or 0.5 percent of tax remitted) and a credit for half the cost of new compliance equipment. Their own business purchases and inventory would be tax-exempt.

The bill taxes 'financial intermediation services' — banking, brokerage, and insurance fees, including implicit fees on interest-bearing accounts and debt — raising costs for savers and borrowers, though the first $10,000 of such fees is exempt each year.

Purchases of a new principal residence would be taxed at 15 percent, payable in annual installments over 30 years with interest, substantially raising the cost of buying a home. Resale of existing homes gets a credit for prior tax paid.

Repealing the income tax and phasing out the IRS would eliminate the income tax filing, software, and advisory work this industry depends on; the bill instead pays accountants and attorneys only when disputes arise.
